# git-epic-workflow

Coordinate several GitHub issues through one `epic/<slug>` branch and one
shared desired/current TLA+ workflow. The epic branch is the integration branch;
ticket branches start from it and target it. The default branch changes only
through the final epic PR.

This skill has three roles:

- **Plan and schedule:** agree the epic's measurable goals, then create the epic
  branch, shared spec workflow, ticket DAG, evaluation tickets, issues, and
  handoff metadata. Read `references/goals-and-evaluation.md`,
  `references/plan-and-schedule.md`, and `references/epic-ticket.md`.
- **Perform one ticket:** detect the epic assignment in an issue and apply its
  overrides to `git-issue-workflow`. Read `references/epic-ticket.md` before
  creating a worktree.
- **Integrate and review a wave:** merge the wave's ticket PRs into the epic
  branch in promotion order, reconcile each ticket worktree's Skill Manager home
  into the project home, then stop and hand the user the review artifact, the
  rendered diff, and the walkthrough. Read `references/human-review.md` and
  `references/worktree-lifecycle.md`.
- **Finalize:** validate the integrated epic, promote the accepted program
  model, close the shared spec workflow, open the epic PR, and — once its merge
  is verified — sweep every worktree the epic created. Read
  `references/finalize.md` and `references/worktree-lifecycle.md`.

## Load-bearing rules

1. **The plan is canonical.** Keep the complete schedule in
   `specs/desired_program_model/ticket_plan.yaml`. GitHub issues mirror it for
   handoff; they do not replace it.
2. **One epic, one branch, one workflow.** Create one `epic/<slug>` from the
   current default-branch tip and scaffold the spec workflow once. Give the
   workflow a unique stable name. Never force-push the epic branch.
3. **Dispatched identities are immutable, including retired work.** Do not
   delete, reorder, rename, or reuse a ticket ID after publishing issue
   assignments; delivery histories and retirement-receipt paths depend on the
   original zero-based plan ordinal and ID. Adding scope creates a new ticket.
   Removing scope preserves the original entry with `status: retired`, bumps
   `schedule_revision`, and records an explicit retirement receipt and affected
   goal disposition (`references/plan-and-schedule.md`).
4. **The epic assignment wins.** Its marker-delimited block overrides ordinary
   `git-issue` instructions that branch from or merge to the default branch.
5. **Ticket agents close one ticket only.** They run `open ticket <id>`, update
   the implementation, specs, spec-unit adapters, Test Graph adapters/nodes,
   record evidence, and run `close ticket <id>`. They never run
   `close_tickets.py` or promote the whole workflow.
6. **Parallel work; serialized promotion.** `depends_on` controls when work may
   start. A separate total `promotion_predecessor` order controls when a ticket
   may rebase onto the latest epic tip, close/promote its ticket, and enter the
   epic branch. The promotion order must be a topological extension of
   `depends_on`; two ticket promotions never integrate concurrently.
7. **Ticket agents stop at PR open; the epic agent merges the wave.** A ticket
   agent stops after pushing a sealed branch and opening a PR whose base is the
   epic branch. It does not merge its own PR, merge to the default branch, or
   close the GitHub issue — it cannot see the wave, so it cannot know whether
   the promotion lane held or a sibling landed on the same file. The **epic
   agent** merges those PRs into `epic/<slug>` in promotion order, one at a
   time, without waiting for a human: the epic branch is an integration branch,
   the merge is reversible, and finalize.md §3 still gates everything before it
   reaches the default branch. A merge conflict is a stop, not a task — it means
   the ticket closed against a tree that no longer exists, so it goes back to
   its agent to reconcile. Read `references/human-review.md` §1.
8. **Only finalization closes the workflow.** After all delivered ticket PRs are
   on the epic branch and every retired ticket has its verified no-delivery
   receipt, the finalizer runs integrated validation, promotes the accepted
   model, closes the workflow, and opens the epic PR against the default branch.
9. **Out-of-scope findings are deferred, not chased.** Agree a deferment policy
   with the user when the epic branch is created. Ticket agents report failure
   cases outside their declared slice to an append-only backlog instead of
   expanding scope to fix them. Read `references/deferment.md`.
10. **A ticket's Skill Manager home is not carried by its PR.** Every worktree an
    epic creates — the epic worktree and each ticket worktree — has its own
    `<worktree>/.skill-manager`, a real copy of the project home. It is
    gitignored, so nothing a ticket agent changed inside it appears in the ticket
    PR, in the epic branch, or in the epic PR. It reaches the tier above only
    through `skill-manager home sync`, and the unit's own repository only through
    `skill-manager unit publish`. An epic cannot finalize until every ticket
    worktree has been through `skill-manager home close-out` — see
    `references/plan-and-schedule.md` §2 and `references/finalize.md` §1b.

    **The epic agent owns that change management.** A ticket agent runs the
    read-only gate and reports its verdict; it never syncs into the project
    home, because that is one shared destination and a ticket agent cannot see
    the tickets it would be racing. The epic agent reconciles each worktree's
    home into `<main-working-tree>/.skill-manager` at wave close — serialized, one
    worktree at a time, reading `held-back` and `conflicted` as decisions rather
    than retries — and is responsible for every worktree being emptied of
    unmerged work before anything is deleted. Read
    `references/worktree-lifecycle.md`.

    **That home does not appear on its own.** The epic branch and every ticket
    worktree path are *declared* by the plan and the assignment — the one case
    the conventional front door's derived path cannot serve. In a home carrying
    the `skt` plugin, one command does the declared pair — worktree at the
    declared path, pinned to the resolved base, WITH its own home, rolled back
    together if the bootstrap fails:

    ```bash
    # skt lives in bin/cli of the home, NOT in skills/ -- it is a plugin.
    SKT="${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/bin/cli/skt"
    [ -x "$SKT" ] || SKT="$(command -v skt)"          # or on PATH
    "$SKT" ticket new <ticket> --base "$commit_oid" --path <declared-worktree>
    ```

    **Check for it at that path.** Measured twice by eval: an agent looked for
    `skt` under `skills/`, did not find it there because it is a plugin, and
    fell through to the hand-run pair below -- reading `wt` and
    `bootstrap-home.sh` and replaying their steps. Both runs had a working
    `skt` in `bin/cli` the whole time. `ls skills/` is the wrong question, and
    the answer to the right one is one `-x` test.

    It applies the index-base pinning conventions (clean slate, OIDs resolved
    once, create-only retention ref, branch from the pinned commit) and refuses
    a retention-ref conflict rather than repinning. Without skt, the same pair
    is two hand-run steps — and `git worktree add` on its own leaves the agent
    writing the operator's global home:

    ```bash
    SKILLS="${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/skills/git-issue-workflow/scripts"

    # ONE chained command, deliberately: the add alone produces a worktree
    # with NO home — the exact hazard measured live in the W2 eval.
    git worktree add <declared-worktree> -b <declared-branch> "$commit_oid" \
      && "$SKILLS/bootstrap-home.sh" --root <declared-worktree>
    ```

    Teardown is one command in every case, because it resolves a ticket by
    searching rather than by the path convention: `skt ticket close <ticket>`,
    or `"$SKILLS/wt" close <ticket>` where skt is absent. A repository that has
    never been given a home makes `bootstrap-home.sh` the *first* thing run in
    it, which is the same one-time per-repository step `wt new` prints as its
    `fix:` line elsewhere.

    **Reaching that by-hand pair is itself a finding — report it.** It is
    written for a home that genuinely has no `skt`, and it *works*, which is
    the whole problem: an agent that merely could not FIND the front door lands
    on it, produces a plausible worktree, and leaves no trace but four tool
    calls where one would have done. Measured four times across the eval suite,
    for four different reasons, and none of the four reported anything. So run
    the `-x` test above first. If it did not resolve, the by-hand pair is
    correct and there is nothing to report. If it resolved and you are on the
    by-hand pair anyway, say which of these you were in:

    - `skt` is installed but was not on `PATH`;
    - you looked where a plugin never is (`skills/`);
    - you found it and it **failed** — quote its `error:` line verbatim;
    - you found it and could not read the home it pointed at.

    All four are front-door defects, not facts about the repository. An epic
    agent has two places to put that line — the wave review artifact
    (`references/human-review.md`) for its own provisioning, and the ticket's
    PR body when a ticket agent reports it — and files it against the skill
    that owns the door: `git-epic-workflow` for the declared-path route above,
    `git-issue-workflow` for `wt`, `skt` for the plugin.
11. **The epic owns whether the homes are CURRENT, and checks before scheduling
    anything.** Every ticket worktree is a *copy* of the project home, and the
    project home is a copy of the root `~/.skill-manager`. Copies do not update
    themselves. So a skill fixed and merged yesterday is still absent from a
    home cloned the day before, and every ticket agent the epic deploys inherits
    that staleness — silently in a home without skt; with the skt plugin
    installed, the session hooks surface it, but the epic must not assume every
    home has them.

    The tool answers this now: `skt check` compares each change-managed unit's
    installed hash against its source's tip and names what is stale and the
    command that pulls it. (`home drift` answers "did anything change *in* this
    home" and exits 0 on a stale one; `home verify` answers "does everything in
    it *resolve*" — neither answers "is this home *current*", which is why the
    check exists.) The epic is still the last point where one check covers every
    ticket that follows, so BEFORE scheduling, run it in both tiers:

    ```bash
    skt check                                     # in the root home
    SKILL_MANAGER_HOME=<repo>/.skill-manager skt check    # and the project home
    ```

    Where skt is not installed, the same comparison by hand:

    ```bash
    for f in "${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}"/installed/*.json; do
      n=$(basename "$f" .json); case "$n" in *.projections) continue;; esac
      python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('$f'));print('$n', (d.get('gitHash') or 'none')[:8])"
    done
    ```

    Any unit behind its merged source gets `skt sync <unit>` (or `skill-manager
    sync <unit>`) in the root home **and** in the project home before the first
    ticket is scheduled —
    not after, because a worktree cloned from a stale project home carries the
    staleness into work you will then have to redo. Sync in dependency order:
    a unit whose `skill-imports` name a file added by another unit fails
    validation with exit 11 if that other unit has not been synced yet, and the
    violation is an artifact of the order, not a real one.

    If the repository has other checkouts with their own homes, they are stale
    too and no command fans out to them. Say so in the epic's kickoff notes
    rather than letting a ticket agent discover it.

    **"Current" is about unit bytes, not derived artifacts, and do not conflate
    the two.** A ticket home *inherits* the artifacts its parent holds and
    *declares* the rest, so `skill-manager artifacts stale` reporting a nonzero
    count in a fresh clone is not staleness this rule is about, and scheduling a
    rebuild for it wastes every ticket's provisioning. The contract — including
    when `skill-manager build <id>` is the right move, and the two wrong
    diagnoses that have already been reached by reading the source instead — is
    stated once at
    `${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/plugins/skt/skills/skt/references/derived-artifacts.md`
    -- which is absent in a home that does not have the skt plugin installed,
    **including, very likely, the project home you are standing in**. When it is
    not there: the page is `skills/skt/references/derived-artifacts.md` in
    `github.com/haydenrear/skill-publisher-skill`, and `skill-manager install
    github:haydenrear/skill-publisher-skill` puts it in the home. Point ticket
    agents at it, and do not paraphrase it into an epic's kickoff notes -- but do
    not leave an agent with a dead link and a prohibition either, which is what
    this paragraph did before the fallback was named.
12. **Every epic states measurable goals; every ticket relates to one.** Ask the
    user what should be measurably better before scaffolding the workflow.
    Record each goal with its metric, harness command, baseline, and target;
    schedule terminal evaluation/perf/integration tickets that decide them; and
    give every other ticket an explicit contribution, expected effect, and local
    signal. The goal relation is the context a ticket agent aims at, so keep it
    specific. Read `references/goals-and-evaluation.md`.
13. **Every wave boundary produces a review, and by default it is a gate.**
    After merging a wave and before handing out any issue URL from the next one,
    write a committed review artifact and walk the user through it: hot spots in
    what landed, decisions made implicitly and guardrails overridden, where the
    bugs probably are, architectural changes worth making — including to the
    epic's own machinery, which lives in gitignored homes and reaches nothing by
    being merged — and the recommended next steps read together with the
    deferred-findings backlog. Then stop and wait. The user may change the
    cadence, drop the gate, or take the merges back; that answer is recorded as
    `review_policy` in the canonical plan, because at finalization a review
    nobody chose to skip is indistinguishable from one that never happened.
    Read `references/human-review.md`.
14. **Worktrees stand until the epic ends, then all of them go in one sweep.**
    Keep every ticket worktree through review — that is what makes the review
    model work — and then remove all of them in one deliberate pass once the
    default-branch merge is verified. The two clocks are deliberate and
    opposite: unit state merges **early**, at wave close, while its author is
    reachable; worktrees are deleted **late**, together. Removal must never be
    the step that carries the merge, because `git worktree remove` deletes a
    gitignored home without asking and succeeds just as quietly whether it held
    a week of skill edits or nothing. Size the disk cost honestly: a home is
    cloned copy-on-write, so a new worktree is nearly free (measured here, 33.7
    MB real for a home `du` calls 1.1 GB), and the real space goes to per-home
    venvs, tools, and divergence as work happens in it. Measure the sweep with
    free space, never with `du`. The epic is not finished while a worktree it
    created is still standing without a recorded reason. Read
    `references/worktree-lifecycle.md`.

## Preconditions

Use this workflow only in a repository already onboarded to both dependencies:

- `specs/program_model` is a complete accepted baseline with Internal and
  External views, adapter mappings, and append-only `specs/.history`.
- `test_graph/` exists and its affected graphs can be discovered.
- No unrelated desired/current workflow is active on the proposed epic branch.
- `gh` authentication and the repository/default branch have been verified.

If the spec baseline or Test Graph project is missing, stop and onboard through
`spec-double-compiler` and `test-graph`; epic kickoff is not onboarding.

Version 1 targets one ordinary Git repository. If `INTEGRATION.md` and
`integration.toml` identify an integration repository, stop rather than mixing
per-constituent fan-out with an unmerged epic branch.

## Scheduling model

Every planned ticket declares:

- stable spec ticket ID and GitHub issue URL;
- `depends_on` and `blocks`;
- a parallel wave;
- conflict keys for production, TLA+, adapters, Test Graph, and workflow data;
- a total `promotion_order` and `promotion_predecessor`;
- the immutable schedule revision and plan commit that produced the assignment;
- exact validation commands and evidence destinations;
- the epic goals it serves, with contribution kind, expected effect, and a
  local signal that predicts the final measurement.

A ticket is ready to **start** only when every dependency PR is merged into
`origin/epic/<slug>` and the review gate on the preceding wave has been answered
(`references/human-review.md` §2). Tickets may share a wave only when neither
reaches the other in the dependency DAG and their conflict keys are disjoint. A ticket is
ready to **promote** only when its promotion predecessor is merged into the
epic branch and the ticket branch has reconciled against that latest tip.

A `retired` ticket remains at its original ordinal as append-only planning
history but is absent from the active dependency, conflict, and promotion
graphs. No undelivered non-retired ticket may depend on, block, or name it as
promotion predecessor. A delivered ticket retains its sealed historical edges,
including edges to a ticket retired by a later amendment; new work skips the
retired entry. `retired` means the owner deliberately removed the work; it is
not synonymous with `done`, and `carried`, `superseded`, or `abandoned` belong
in `retirement.resolution`, never directly in `status`.

Evaluation tickets are ordinary tickets whose slice is measurement. Each one
depends on every ticket contributing to the goals it owns and promotes after
them, so the harness runs on the integrated result rather than a partial one.

`depends_on` is planning metadata; `tla-spec-dev` does not enforce the DAG.
Validate missing references, self-dependencies, cycles, readiness, and conflict
keys before dispatch. Validate each issue assignment against its current
canonical plan entry before starting and again before promotion.

## Operating flow

### Start or resume an epic

1. Follow `references/plan-and-schedule.md`.
2. Ask the user what should be measurably better when the epic is done, before
   scaffolding the workflow. Turn the answers into goals with metrics,
   harnesses, baselines, and targets, and schedule the evaluation ticket(s)
   that decide them (`references/goals-and-evaluation.md`).
3. Use `git-issue` for discovery and issue authoring. For existing issues,
   preserve their bodies and replace only the marker-delimited epic assignment.
4. Agree the deferment policy with the user before dispatch and record it in
   the canonical plan (`references/deferment.md`). In the same conversation,
   agree the review cadence, whether the wave review gates the next wave, and
   who merges ticket PRs into the epic branch; record that as `review_policy`
   (`references/human-review.md` §2).
5. Validate every rendered assignment before handing out its issue URL —
   `scripts/validate_assignment.py`, against the issue body as GitHub now holds
   it, with `--expect-ticket` and `--expect-epic-branch`. The schema is
   specified here, rendered by `git-issue`, and parsed by `git-issue-workflow`,
   so a `pr_base` that is not the epic branch fails here and an omitted policy
   block or placeholder shows up as a short warning. Only wrong-branch,
   wrong-ticket, and missing-location errors block; `--force` (or
   `SKILL_GATES=off`) passes those too when you have decided they do not apply.
   Never rewrite a plan or re-scope a ticket just to silence a warning.
6. Commit and push the epic branch before handing out any issue URL.
7. Report the epic branch/tip, workflow name, the goal table, and a table of
   issue URL, ticket ID, dependencies, wave, promotion predecessor, and goals
   served. Hand out only ready issue URLs. When recommending the next ticket,
   present pending deferred findings alongside it and triage them with the user.

### Work an epic issue

1. Read the issue before touching git. If it contains the epic assignment
   markers, follow `references/epic-ticket.md`; do not apply the ordinary
   default-branch closeout from `git-issue-workflow`.
2. Read the assignment's goal entries before implementing; the declared
   expected effect is the result the change is aiming at. Work and validate in
   the ticket worktree, run the declared local signal before close, and report
   it against the expected effect. Classify every failure case found in
   validation or review against the ticket's declared slice; defer, batch, or
   escalate out-of-scope findings under the epic's deferment policy rather than
   widening the ticket to fix them or to chase a metric.
3. Wait for the declared promotion predecessor, reconcile the latest epic tip,
   close only the assigned spec ticket with evidence, push, and open the PR
   against the epic branch.
4. Stop at PR open. Treat the committed close record and evidence as sealed; a
   semantic review change becomes an explicit amendment ticket rather than an
   edit to append-only history.

### Integrate and review a wave

1. Merge the wave's ticket PRs into `epic/<slug>` in promotion order, one at a
   time, verifying checks and assignment/plan equality before each merge. Stop
   and return the ticket to its agent on a conflict, a failing REQUIRED matrix
   entry, or a pending blocking finding.
2. Reconcile each ticket worktree's Skill Manager home into the project home,
   one worktree at a time, and check every worktree for uncommitted, stashed,
   unpushed, or epic-unmerged work. Update the worktree ledger
   (`references/worktree-lifecycle.md` §3–§4). Leave the worktrees standing.
3. Build the review artifact over the whole wave range and commit it under the
   plan's `review_policy.artifact_root`, with the diff stat, the patch, the
   merge record, and the ledger beside it.
4. Render the diff visualization and walk the user through it quickly — what the
   wave was for, the design decisions, the intuition, where the bugs probably
   are, what was decided for them, and the ask.
5. Wait for the user's answer unless the plan waived the gate, then record that
   answer in the artifact and dispatch the next wave — amended if the review
   changed the plan. Read `references/human-review.md`.

### Finalize an epic

Follow `references/finalize.md`. Do not infer that “all agents are done” from
open PRs or local branches: verify each delivered ticket's merged PR and
close-history entry separately from each retired ticket's canonical retirement
receipt. A PR/history cannot substitute for a retirement receipt, and a receipt
cannot be presented as delivered work. Report every declared goal as baseline
→ measured → target with a verdict or its explicit retirement disposition; a
missed goal is a decision for the user, and a silently unmeasured goal is not an
acceptable close.

## Boundaries

- Do not launch or monitor ticket agents. Return ready issue URLs; the user
  starts agents and invokes this skill again for status or finalization.
- Do not silently alter dependencies, ticket order, or conflict ownership after
  dispatch.
- Do not delete an unwanted dispatched ticket or mark it `carried`,
  `superseded`, or `abandoned` as though those were delivery statuses. Retire it
  through the canonical plan amendment and receipt flow.
- Do not invent goals, targets, or baselines the user did not agree to, and do
  not edit a target so a measured result passes. Report the run that happened.
- Do not use `--accept-new` for ticket close or workflow finalization. Reconcile
  current and desired explicitly so validation proves the promoted state.
- Do not use closing keywords in ticket PRs. Use `Refs #<issue>` and reserve
  issue-closing references for the final epic PR.
- Do not bypass branch protection or external review gates. Merging a ticket PR
  into the epic branch is the epic agent's job; merging the epic PR into the
  default branch is the user's, and needs their explicit authorization.
- Do not dispatch the next wave before the review the plan's `review_policy`
  declares, and do not treat silence as approval.
- Do not fix on the epic branch what a review surfaces, and do not implement the
  architectural changes a review recommends. Both re-enter as tickets.
- Do not remove a worktree before the epic's default-branch merge is verified,
  and do not remove one whose home has not been reconciled or whose tree still
  holds uncommitted, stashed, unpushed, or epic-unmerged work. Never `rm -rf` a
  worktree, and never reach for `wt close --force` to finish faster.
- Do not leave the sweep undone. An epic that skips it has moved its disk cost
  onto the next epic, which is the one that will run out of space.

## Reference map

| Task | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Create/resume branch, workflow, DAG, and issues | `references/plan-and-schedule.md` |
| Agree goals, baselines, and evaluation tickets | `references/goals-and-evaluation.md` |
| Author or execute the epic assignment | `references/epic-ticket.md` |
| Merge a wave, build the review artifact, walk the user through it | `references/human-review.md` |
| Reconcile ticket homes, keep the ledger, sweep the worktrees | `references/worktree-lifecycle.md` |
| Validate, promote, close, and open the epic PR | `references/finalize.md` |
| Classify, defer, batch, and triage failure cases | `references/deferment.md` |
| Deciding whether a ticket home's `declared-only` artifacts need rebuilding | `${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/plugins/skt/skills/skt/references/derived-artifacts.md` — skt owns it; this skill does not restate it, and it is absent in a home without skt |

**One word, two meanings — do not confuse them.** In *this* skill "artifact"
almost always means the **wave review artifact** under `review.artifact_root`,
which a human reads. A **derived artifact** is a thing a Skill Manager home
produced — a CLI shim, a venv, a projection — and it is the skt page above.
Nothing in the review artifact's lifecycle is affected by `artifacts list`, and
"rebuild the artifact" is never an instruction this skill gives.

1	# Goals and evaluation
2	
3	An epic exists to move something measurable. Tickets that only reference their
4	own slice optimize local correctness and leave the epic's actual outcome
5	unmeasured — every ticket passes, the epic ships, and nobody can say whether the
6	thing got faster, more accurate, or more reliable.
7	
8	The fix is one primitive: an epic declares **goals**, one or more terminal
9	**evaluation tickets** own the harness that decides them, and **every ticket
10	declares how it relates to at least one goal**. That relation is load-bearing
11	context: it tells the ticket agent what result its change is supposed to
12	produce, which cheap local signal predicts it, and which final measurement it
13	will be judged by.
14	
15	Goals are agreed with the user at epic creation, alongside the deferment policy
16	(`deferment.md`). Do not infer them from the codebase and do not default them.
17	
18	## What counts as a goal
19	
20	A goal is a specific, falsifiable claim about the program after the epic, with
21	a named instrument that decides it. Write goals as outcomes, not as work.
22	
23	| Not a goal | Goal |
24	| --- | --- |
25	| "Refactor the ingest path" | "p99 ingest latency ≤ 250ms at 5k rps, throughput not regressed" |
26	| "Improve retrieval" | "Answer-match eval ≥ 0.82 on `evals/retrieval_v3.jsonl`, from 0.71" |
27	| "Add integration tests" | "The `epicIntegration` graph passes end to end with no skipped nodes" |
28	
29	Goal kinds:
30	
31	- **`perf`** — latency, throughput, memory, cost; needs a baseline run and a
32	  target expressed against it.
33	- **`eval`** — accuracy/quality judged against a fixed artifact set; needs a
34	  pinned dataset and scorer version, or — for a judged instrument — a pinned
35	  rubric version and a stated judging setup.
36	- **`integration`** — a named end-to-end Test Graph or system path passing under
37	  realistic composition, not per-ticket units.
38	- **`quality`** — an invariant/coverage/robustness property with a deciding
39	  command (TLC model, fuzz budget, conformance suite).
40	
41	Every goal names one deciding instrument. A goal nobody can decide is a slogan;
42	either find the harness, schedule a wave-1 ticket that builds it, or drop the
43	goal.
44	
45	### The instrument does not have to be a command
46	
47	For a long time this file said "one deciding command", and its only worked
48	example was a benchmark script. That framing is too narrow, and the project's
49	own flagship consumer already runs outside it: `tla-spec-dev`'s
50	`ports-as-adapters` epic declares goals whose harness reads
51	
52	> the HP-01-shaped seeded catalogue extended with adapter-internal faults, run
53	> against real and fake wirings, **scored by two blind judges**
54	
55	which is a procedure, not a command line. That repository moved to judged
56	scoring deliberately and on evidence, and states the reason itself: *"A number
57	computed from the artifact can be optimized by editing the artifact. A
58	judgement that must cite the artifact can only be satisfied by changing what
59	the artifact is"* (`tla-spec-dev/references/eval_scorecard.md`). That file is
60	the worked example of a judged instrument and **the sole authority on its own
61	dimensions, anchors, scoring rules, judging protocol, storage, sealing and
62	history rules**. This file cites it and restates none of them.
63	
64	So a `harness` is whatever **decides the goal reproducibly and independently of
65	the person hoping it passed**. Three shapes all qualify:
66	
67	- **a command** — a benchmark, an eval scorer, a graph run. Write the exact
68	  invocation;
69	- **a judged procedure** — an artifact scored against a versioned rubric by
70	  judges who cite the artifact, blind to arm where arms exist. Write what is
71	  scored, by how many judges, under which rubric version, and where the
72	  evidence lands;
73	- **a mixed instrument** — measured figures recorded beside a judged score, read
74	  together rather than combined. How the two are reconciled is the instrument's
75	  rule to state, not this file's.
76	
77	What is still forbidden is an instrument nobody can execute at all. "The design
78	feels cleaner" names no instrument; "scored against `<rubric>` version N by two
79	blind judges, results under `<evidence_root>`" names one, and the fact that a
80	human runs it does not make it unfalsifiable.
81	
82	**Name the instrument; do not copy it.** Write which rubric, which version, how
83	many judges, and where the evidence lands — and then link the rubric. Never
84	restate its dimensions, its anchors, its scoring rules or its comparability
85	rules here. A rubric's own repository versions those and executes checks over
86	them; a copy in this file is covered by nothing and will drift. `tla-spec-dev`
87	learned this by measurement: a charter there restated a table of judged results
88	and two of its rows were wrong, read forward across a change to the instrument
89	before anyone noticed.
90	
91	**A round that calls itself blind must say what its judges received.** Blindness
92	to the packet is not blindness to the operator's conclusions. An agent harness
93	can inject persistent memory, the repository's recent commit subjects, session
94	hooks and an installed-tooling listing into a dispatched judge *before it makes
95	any tool call*, so no forbidden-reading list written inside the dispatch can
96	reach them. Measured on Claude Code: judges dispatched from the repository
97	received the auto-memory index verbatim and the five most recent commit
98	subjects; one, asked before opening any packet, reported that it arrived
99	carrying not only the expected answer but the expected *distribution*, and named
100	the temptation to reproduce it.
101	
102	**It is fixable, and the fix is two halves — neither sufficient alone.** On that
103	harness, `--safe-mode` removes auto-memory, hooks, project skills and MCP but
104	**not** the repository status block, so a judge run at the repository still
105	receives the commit subjects; dispatching from a directory outside any git
106	repository removes those but leaves the session hook and skill listing standing.
107	Both together measured clean. Do not read that as a settled recipe: the flag's
108	own help does not name auto-memory, so a round leaning on it leans on
109	undocumented behaviour, and the honest practice is to **verify rather than trust
110	it** — record the digest of whatever memory file the round was supposed to
111	exclude, and ask each judge to report what it received before it opens anything.
112	
113	So, beside the scores, record which dispatch path was used and what the judges
114	reported receiving. Where a round could not be made blind, print the
115	contamination note next to the number: withdrawing the number or dropping the
116	word *blind* silently both destroy the record of what was actually measured.
117	This is a disclosure obligation a reader can check, deliberately not a gate.
118	
119	### Not every target is a number
120	
121	A target states what counts as success. Usually that is a threshold, but two
122	legitimate shapes are not:
123	
124	- **A multi-clause target.** `GOAL-port-reach` targets "the same adapter-internal
125	  fault dies on at least one generated instrument, **and** no positive control is
126	  red" — two independent clauses that can settle differently, and did.
127	- **A goal with deliberately no numeric target**, where the epic is building the
128	  instrument itself. `GOAL-complexity-measurable` says it outright: *"NO TARGET
129	  ON THE NUMBER ITSELF — a threshold before anything can produce a number would
130	  be inventing the answer."* Its baseline is "no such instrument exists". A
131	  first-measurement goal is decided by whether the instrument runs and
132	  discriminates, not by a figure chosen before anything could produce one.
133	
134	Write either plainly in `target`. Do not manufacture a threshold to make the
135	field look conventional — an invented number is the failure this whole primitive
136	exists to prevent, and it is worse than an honest "no target on the number".
137	
138	## Ask the user at epic creation
139	
140	Ask before scaffolding the workflow, and ask concretely:
141	
142	> What should be measurably better when this epic is done? For each outcome I
143	> need: the metric, the instrument that decides it — a command, or a judged
144	> procedure with its rubric — its value today, and the
145	> threshold that counts as success. If a harness does not exist yet, I will
146	> schedule a wave-1 ticket to build it and measure the baseline before the
147	> tickets that change behavior.
148	>
149	> I will add a final evaluation ticket that runs those measurements on the
150	> integrated epic branch, and every other ticket will declare how it moves each
151	> metric so its agent knows what result it is aiming at.
152	
153	Push back on unmeasurable answers once, offering the nearest measurable form.
154	If the user genuinely has no measurable outcome (pure refactor, docs, plumbing),
155	record that decision explicitly rather than inventing a metric:
156	
157	```yaml
158	epic_goals: []
159	goals_waived: "<user's reason: no behavioral delta; correctness held by existing suites>"
160	```
161	
162	The validator warns on a waived or missing goal set; it does not block. A waived
163	epic still runs its normal ticket validation matrices.
164	
165	## Baselines
166	
167	A target without a baseline cannot be evaluated — "p99 ≤ 250ms" is unfalsifiable
168	if nobody knows today's number.
169	
170	- **Harness exists** — measure at epic kickoff on the freshly created epic
171	  branch, before any ticket lands. Commit the measurement under the epic
172	  evidence root and record its value and commit SHA in the goal.
173	- **Harness does not exist** — schedule a wave-1 ticket whose slice is the
174	  harness plus the baseline run. Every behavior-changing ticket depends on it.
175	  Until it merges, the goal's `baseline.value` stays `unmeasured` and the
176	  validator warns.
177	- **Harness is judged and this subject has never been scored under it** — the
178	  instrument existing is not a baseline. Run it at epic kickoff on the epic
179	  branch, before any ticket lands, exactly as for a command harness; seal that
180	  run and record its card as the baseline. A judged instrument that has been
181	  run on other subjects, or in other epics, has measured something else. If a
182	  kickoff round is not affordable, `unmeasured` with the reason is the honest
183	  answer and the goal stays legal — a goal that cannot be scored is not a goal
184	  that fails.
185	
186	Never take the baseline after the first behavioral ticket has merged; that
187	measures the epic against itself.
188	
189	**A judged baseline is a prior scored run, not a recollection.** Where the
190	instrument is a judged one, `baseline.value` cites the sealed card that produced
191	the number and `baseline.evidence` points at it, so the comparison is against a
192	record that cannot be edited afterwards. Two consequences follow, both learned
193	the hard way in `ports-as-adapters`:
194	
195	- **A baseline can be superseded before the epic starts.** A wider or repaired
196	  instrument may have re-measured the same thing since. Move the bar to the
197	  newer number, say which run it came from, and leave the superseded run sealed
198	  and unedited on the record — measuring divergence against a weaker instrument
199	  credits movement the better one absorbs.
200	- **A number measured on one instrument is not comparable across a repair of
201	  that instrument.** If the instrument changed between baseline and measurement,
202	  say so and treat the movement as a fact about the instrument until proven
203	  otherwise. `tla-spec-dev` executes this as a rule and an audit; the general
204	  point is that "the number moved" and "the thing got better" are different
205	  claims.
206	
207	**For a judged goal, `baseline.evidence` is the card, not the folder it sits
208	in.** Point it at the sealed card that produced the number, or — where the

# Goals and evaluation

An epic exists to move something measurable. Tickets that only reference their
own slice optimize local correctness and leave the epic's actual outcome
unmeasured — every ticket passes, the epic ships, and nobody can say whether the
thing got faster, more accurate, or more reliable.

The fix is one primitive: an epic declares **goals**, one or more terminal
**evaluation tickets** own the harness that decides them, and **every ticket
declares how it relates to at least one goal**. That relation is load-bearing
context: it tells the ticket agent what result its change is supposed to
produce, which cheap local signal predicts it, and which final measurement it
will be judged by.

Goals are agreed with the user at epic creation, alongside the deferment policy
(`deferment.md`). Do not infer them from the codebase and do not default them.

## What counts as a goal

A goal is a specific, falsifiable claim about the program after the epic, with
a named instrument that decides it. Write goals as outcomes, not as work.

| Not a goal | Goal |
| --- | --- |
| "Refactor the ingest path" | "p99 ingest latency ≤ 250ms at 5k rps, throughput not regressed" |
| "Improve retrieval" | "Answer-match eval ≥ 0.82 on `evals/retrieval_v3.jsonl`, from 0.71" |
| "Add integration tests" | "The `epicIntegration` graph passes end to end with no skipped nodes" |

Goal kinds:

- **`perf`** — latency, throughput, memory, cost; needs a baseline run and a
  target expressed against it.
- **`eval`** — accuracy/quality judged against a fixed artifact set; needs a
  pinned dataset and scorer version, or — for a judged instrument — a pinned
  rubric version and a stated judging setup.
- **`integration`** — a named end-to-end Test Graph or system path passing under
  realistic composition, not per-ticket units.
- **`quality`** — an invariant/coverage/robustness property with a deciding
  command (TLC model, fuzz budget, conformance suite).

Every goal names one deciding instrument. A goal nobody can decide is a slogan;
either find the harness, schedule a wave-1 ticket that builds it, or drop the
goal.

### The instrument does not have to be a command

For a long time this file said "one deciding command", and its only worked
example was a benchmark script. That framing is too narrow, and the project's
own flagship consumer already runs outside it: `tla-spec-dev`'s
`ports-as-adapters` epic declares goals whose harness reads

> the HP-01-shaped seeded catalogue extended with adapter-internal faults, run
> against real and fake wirings, **scored by two blind judges**

which is a procedure, not a command line. That repository moved to judged
scoring deliberately and on evidence, and states the reason itself: *"A number
computed from the artifact can be optimized by editing the artifact. A
judgement that must cite the artifact can only be satisfied by changing what
the artifact is"* (`tla-spec-dev/references/eval_scorecard.md`). That file is
the worked example of a judged instrument and **the sole authority on its own
dimensions, anchors, scoring rules, judging protocol, storage, sealing and
history rules**. This file cites it and restates none of them.

So a `harness` is whatever **decides the goal reproducibly and independently of
the person hoping it passed**. Three shapes all qualify:

- **a command** — a benchmark, an eval scorer, a graph run. Write the exact
  invocation;
- **a judged procedure** — an artifact scored against a versioned rubric by
  judges who cite the artifact, blind to arm where arms exist. Write what is
  scored, by how many judges, under which rubric version, and where the
  evidence lands;
- **a mixed instrument** — measured figures recorded beside a judged score, read
  together rather than combined. How the two are reconciled is the instrument's
  rule to state, not this file's.

What is still forbidden is an instrument nobody can execute at all. "The design
feels cleaner" names no instrument; "scored against `<rubric>` version N by two
blind judges, results under `<evidence_root>`" names one, and the fact that a
human runs it does not make it unfalsifiable.

**Name the instrument; do not copy it.** Write which rubric, which version, how
many judges, and where the evidence lands — and then link the rubric. Never
restate its dimensions, its anchors, its scoring rules or its comparability
rules here. A rubric's own repository versions those and executes checks over
them; a copy in this file is covered by nothing and will drift. `tla-spec-dev`
learned this by measurement: a charter there restated a table of judged results
and two of its rows were wrong, read forward across a change to the instrument
before anyone noticed.

**A round that calls itself blind must say what its judges received.** Blindness
to the packet is not blindness to the operator's conclusions. An agent harness
can inject persistent memory, the repository's recent commit subjects, session
hooks and an installed-tooling listing into a dispatched judge *before it makes
any tool call*, so no forbidden-reading list written inside the dispatch can
reach them. Measured on Claude Code: judges dispatched from the repository
received the auto-memory index verbatim and the five most recent commit
subjects; one, asked before opening any packet, reported that it arrived
carrying not only the expected answer but the expected *distribution*, and named
the temptation to reproduce it.

**It is fixable, and the fix is two halves — neither sufficient alone.** On that
harness, `--safe-mode` removes auto-memory, hooks, project skills and MCP but
**not** the repository status block, so a judge run at the repository still
receives the commit subjects; dispatching from a directory outside any git
repository removes those but leaves the session hook and skill listing standing.
Both together measured clean. Do not read that as a settled recipe: the flag's
own help does not name auto-memory, so a round leaning on it leans on
undocumented behaviour, and the honest practice is to **verify rather than trust
it** — record the digest of whatever memory file the round was supposed to
exclude, and ask each judge to report what it received before it opens anything.

So, beside the scores, record which dispatch path was used and what the judges
reported receiving. Where a round could not be made blind, print the
contamination note next to the number: withdrawing the number or dropping the
word *blind* silently both destroy the record of what was actually measured.
This is a disclosure obligation a reader can check, deliberately not a gate.

### Not every target is a number

A target states what counts as success. Usually that is a threshold, but two
legitimate shapes are not:

- **A multi-clause target.** `GOAL-port-reach` targets "the same adapter-internal
  fault dies on at least one generated instrument, **and** no positive control is
  red" — two independent clauses that can settle differently, and did.
- **A goal with deliberately no numeric target**, where the epic is building the
  instrument itself. `GOAL-complexity-measurable` says it outright: *"NO TARGET
  ON THE NUMBER ITSELF — a threshold before anything can produce a number would
  be inventing the answer."* Its baseline is "no such instrument exists". A
  first-measurement goal is decided by whether the instrument runs and
  discriminates, not by a figure chosen before anything could produce one.

field look conventional — an invented number is the failure this whole primitive
exists to prevent, and it is worse than an honest "no target on the number".

> threshold that counts as success. If a harness does not exist yet, I will
> schedule a wave-1 ticket to build it and measure the baseline before the
> tickets that change behavior.
>

> integrated epic branch, and every other ticket will declare how it moves each
> metric so its agent knows what result it is aiming at.

```yaml
epic_goals: []
goals_waived: "<user's reason: no behavioral delta; correctness held by existing suites>"
```

  branch, before any ticket lands. Commit the measurement under the epic
  evidence root and record its value and commit SHA in the goal.
- **Harness does not exist** — schedule a wave-1 ticket whose slice is the
  harness plus the baseline run. Every behavior-changing ticket depends on it.

1	# Plan and schedule an epic
2	
3	Use this reference when creating a new epic or reconciling a partially planned
4	one. Discovery and issue content still follow `git-issue`; this reference adds
5	the shared branch, spec workflow, and schedule.
6	
7	## 1. Preflight
8	
9	Confirm all of these before writing:
10	
11	```bash
12	gh auth status
13	gh repo view --json nameWithOwner,defaultBranchRef
14	git status --short --branch
15	git fetch origin
16	ls specs/program_model specs/.history test_graph
17	```
18	
19	Inspect `specs/program_model/spec_manifest.yaml`, both TLA+ views, action and
20	adapter mappings, active spec directories, the existing graph plans, and the
21	latest relevant history. Stop if the baseline is incomplete or an unrelated
22	`specs/current` / `specs/desired_program_model` workflow is active on the branch
23	lineage.
24	
25	For a resumed epic, first read its remote branch, ticket plan, assignment blocks,
26	and ticket PRs. Reconcile those artifacts instead of scaffolding again.
27	
28	## 2. Create the epic integration branch
29	
30	### Worktree provisioning conventions (index-base pinning)
31	
32	Every worktree this skill creates — the epic worktree here and every ticket
33	worktree in `epic-ticket.md` — follows these conventions so its base is
34	immutable and reproducible (index platforms such as commit-diff-context
35	snapshot branching consume these OIDs as base-snapshot identity):
36	
37	1. **Clean slate** — `git status --porcelain` empty before provisioning;
38	   stop and reconcile otherwise.
39	2. **Resolve the base rev to object IDs once** — capture
40	   `commit_oid=$(git rev-parse <base-ref>)` and
41	   `tree_oid=$(git rev-parse "<base-ref>^{tree}")`; record them; never
42	   re-resolve the branch name afterwards.
43	3. **Retention ref** — create-only
44	   `git update-ref refs/index-bases/<repo-id>/<tree_oid> <commit_oid> ""`;
45	   an existing ref pointing at a different commit is a hard error. Reserved
46	   namespace, never public tags.
47	4. **Branch from the pinned commit**, not from the moving ref name.
48	
49	Choose a short stable slug and create a dedicated epic worktree from the fetched
50	default-branch tip:
51	
52	`skt` is a plugin, so it is never under a home's `skills/`; test it by path:
53	
54	```bash
55	SMH="${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}"
56	test -x "$SMH/bin/cli/skt"        # -> use the one command below
57	```
58	
59	Where it resolves, one command applies every convention below — clean-slate
60	check, OIDs resolved once, create-only retention ref, branch from the pinned
61	commit — and gives the worktree its own home in the same breath, rolling both
62	back if the bootstrap fails:
63	
64	```bash
65	git fetch origin
66	skt ticket new epic-<slug> --base origin/<default-branch> --path ../wt-epic-<slug>
67	cd ../wt-epic-<slug>
68	```
69	
70	(The branch it creates is `feature/epic-<slug>`; rename with `git branch -m
71	epic/<slug>` if the plan declares the bare epic name, or pass the resolved
72	`commit_oid` as `--base`.) Without skt, the same conventions by hand — and if
73	you are here because the front door was not *found* rather than not *present*,
74	that is a front-door defect: report it under `SKILL.md` rule 10, *Reaching that
75	by-hand pair is itself a finding*.
76	
77	```bash
78	git fetch origin
79	test -z "$(git status --porcelain)" || { echo "dirty tree — reconcile first"; exit 1; }
80	commit_oid=$(git rev-parse origin/<default-branch>)
81	tree_oid=$(git rev-parse "origin/<default-branch>^{tree}")
82	git update-ref "refs/index-bases/$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")/${tree_oid}" "$commit_oid" ""
83	git worktree add ../wt-epic-<slug> -b epic/<slug> "$commit_oid"
84	cd ../wt-epic-<slug>
85	# NOT DONE YET: this worktree has NO home until the bootstrap under
86	# "Skill Manager homes" below runs — that block is part of THIS step,
87	# not optional reading (the W2 eval measured an agent stopping here).
88	```
89	
90	Record the starting SHA (`commit_oid`). Never create ticket branches from the
91	primary checkout or from the default branch once the epic exists. Never
92	force-push `epic/<slug>`.
93	
94	### Skill Manager homes: what an epic is actually fanning out
95	
96	An epic is the first place the three-tier home model becomes a *scheduling*
97	concern, so decide it here rather than discovering it at finalization.
98	
99	```
100	root       ~/.skill-manager              where the operator installs
101	   |  copy
102	project    <repo>/.skill-manager         ONE per repository — the shared destination
103	   |  copy                               for every worktree below
104	worktree   <worktree>/.skill-manager     one per ticket, and one for the epic worktree
105	```
106	
107	Each tier is a **real copy, not a symlink**, and that is the load-bearing part for
108	you: an epic runs several ticket agents at once, and a symlink farm would make
109	their homes one shared object, so two agents editing "their" copy of a skill would
110	be editing each other's, last writer winning silently. Copies buy you the
111	parallelism the whole scheduling model assumes.
112	
113	Give the epic worktree its own home before running anything that installs, syncs,
114	binds, or resolves — those all write into whatever `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` names, and
115	before the local home exists that is the operator's global home:
116	
117	```bash
118	# the skt path above already did this; by hand it is:
119	"${SKILL_MANAGER_HOME:-$HOME/.skill-manager}/skills/git-issue-workflow/scripts/bootstrap-home.sh" \
120	  --root ../wt-epic-<slug>
121	```
122	
123	That path is the resolution, not a placeholder: an installed unit's files live at
124	`$SKILL_MANAGER_HOME/skills/<unit>/`, and the `:-` fallback makes the same line
125	work from a bare shell. If this repository has never been given a home of its own,
126	this is also the command that gives it one — run it with `--root <repo-root>`
127	first, once, then again for the worktree.
128	
129	Then note two things about the schedule you are about to write:
130	
131	- **`conflict_keys` do not cover units in a home.** They partition *tracked files*
132	  under lane names the plan chooses — `production`, `tla`, `adapters`,
133	  `test_graph` and `workflow` are common examples, not a required set, and the
134	  validators accept any lane name. A skill unit lives in a home,
135	  which is gitignored, so two tickets in the same wave can have perfectly disjoint
136	  conflict keys and still both improve `test-graph` in their own homes. Neither
137	  edit is in either PR. **You** reconcile both into the one project home at that
138	  wave's close (`references/worktree-lifecycle.md` §3), in serial, and the second
139	  one comes back **held back** rather than overwritten — a conflict you resolve,
140	  not a silent loss. That is the designed outcome, but it is work you scheduled
141	  without meaning to. If you expect a wave to touch the same unit, say so in the
142	  assignment and have one ticket own it.
143	- **Publishing beats chaining.** `home sync` only moves an edit up one tier. An
144	  improvement that should reach other repositories has to go to the unit's own
145	  git repo via `skill-manager unit publish`; a chain-only route would need the same
146	  merge performed twice and would still never reach a sibling project.
147	- **The schedule has a disk cost, but not the one `du` reports.** Homes are
148	  cloned copy-on-write, so a wave of six worktrees does not cost six project
149	  homes — measured here, cloning a home `du` calls 1.1 GB moved free space by
150	  33.7 MB. The space goes instead to per-home venvs and tools and to divergence
151	  as each worktree is worked in, so the cost grows with *activity*, not with
152	  wave width, and it accrues until the epic's final sweep. Check headroom with
153	  free space before writing the waves, and never size a schedule off `du`:
154	
155	  ```bash
156	  df -h <repo-root>
157	  ```
158	
159	  If the headroom is thin, the answer is a narrower wave or an earlier sweep of
160	  delivered tickets, decided with the user
161	  (`references/worktree-lifecycle.md` §1, §6).
162	
163	## 3. Discover the whole change
164	
165	Use the `git-issue` discovery sequence once for the epic and then refine it per
166	ticket. Identify:
167	
168	- target program state, Internal/External actions, variables, and invariants;
169	- production paths and symbols;
170	- spec-unit adapters and conformance tests;
171	- Test Graph bindings, node IDs, composition, and context keys;
172	- acceptance commands and evidence paths;
173	- true ordering dependencies and potential write conflicts.
174	
175	The desired model describes the final whole-program state. A ticket desired
176	model later describes the whole-program state after that ticket, not a feature
177	fragment.
178	
179	While discovering, inventory what already measures this program: benchmark
180	scripts, eval datasets and scorers, perf-marked test suites, end-to-end Test
181	Graph graphs, and any dashboards or saved baselines. That inventory is the raw
182	material for the goals agreed in step 3a — goals are cheapest when an existing
183	harness already decides them.
184	
185	## 3a. Agree the epic goals
186	
187	Before scaffolding the workflow, ask the user what should be measurably better
188	when the epic is done. This is a required decision, like the deferment policy;
189	do not infer goals from the codebase and do not default them.
190	
191	Ask for each outcome: the metric, the command that measures it, today's value,
192	and the threshold that counts as success. Then:
193	
194	- write each answer as a goal in the schema from `goals-and-evaluation.md`;
195	- measure the baseline now, on the fresh epic branch, whenever the harness
196	  already exists, and commit it under the epic evidence root;
197	- schedule a wave-1 harness+baseline ticket when it does not;
198	- schedule the terminal evaluation ticket(s) that run the harnesses on the
199	  integrated epic and decide each goal;
200	- give every other ticket a goal relation — contribution kind, expected effect,
201	  and a local signal it can run in its own worktree.
202	
203	If the user has no measurable outcome, record `epic_goals: []` with a
204	`goals_waived` reason rather than inventing a metric. Read
205	`references/goals-and-evaluation.md` for goal kinds, baselines, contribution
206	kinds, the evaluation-ticket contract, and reporting.
207	
208	## 4. Scaffold the shared workflow once
209	
210	Choose stable ticket IDs before scaffolding. Use the first ticket only as the
211	CLI seed:
212	
213	```bash
214	tla-spec-dev --spec-root specs scaffold workflow <first-ticket-id> "<epic title>"
215	```
216	
217	Then replace the placeholder planning data with the complete epic:
218	
219	- set a unique workflow `name` / `status.workflow` derived from the epic slug;
220	- make `specs/current` the complete accepted starting model;
221	- author `specs/desired_program_model` as the complete target model;
222	- expand `ticket_plan.yaml` to every stable ticket;
223	- add an integer `schedule_revision` that changes whenever IDs, dependency
224	  edges, waves, promotion order, conflict ownership, or validation scope changes;
225	- add the `epic_goals` block agreed in step 3a;
226	- add the `deferment_policy` block agreed in step 4a;
227	- add the `review_policy` block agreed in step 4b;
228	- remove placeholder actions, scopes, commands, and assertions.
229	
230	Do not run `open ticket` on the epic branch. Each ticket agent opens exactly its
231	own workspace on its ticket branch.
232	
233	Keep the generated ticket schema and add these scheduling fields to each ticket:
234	
235	```yaml
236	github_issue: "https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<number>"
237	schedule_revision: 1
238	depends_on: []
239	blocks: []
240	wave: 1
241	promotion_order: 10
242	promotion_predecessor: null
243	role: implementation          # implementation | evaluation
244	conflict_keys:
245	  production: []
246	  tla: []
247	  adapters: []
248	  test_graph: []
249	  workflow: []
250	goals:
251	  - goal: "<goal-id>"
252	    contribution: direct      # direct | enabling | guard
253	    expected_effect: "<direction and magnitude, or 'none — enabling only'>"
254	    local_signal: "<cheap in-worktree command, or 'N/A: reason'>"
255	```
256	
257	Evaluation tickets add `role: evaluation` and `owns_goals: ["<goal-id>"]`, and
258	depend on every ticket contributing to the goals they own.
259	
260	## 4a. Agree the deferment policy
261	
262	Before any issue is dispatched, ask the user how ticket agents must handle
263	failure cases they find outside their assigned slice. This is a required
264	decision, not a default to assume silently — unbounded in-ticket bug fixing is
265	the main way epic tickets lose their semantic boundary.
266	
267	Ask one question with the concrete tradeoff:
268	
269	> Ticket agents will find real defects outside their assigned slice. How should
270	> they handle them?
271	>
272	> - **batch** (recommended) — record to the backlog, keep working the assigned
273	>   slice, triage between waves and at finalization;
274	> - **ask** — record, then stop and ask you per finding whether to open a ticket
275	>   now or batch it;
276	> - **inline** — allowed to fix within their own conflict keys, still recorded.
277	>
278	> Blocking findings (the ticket's REQUIRED validation cannot pass without
279	> touching another surface) **escalate** to you by default; say so if you would
280	> rather be asked to authorize an inline fix instead.
281	
282	Record the answer, a per-ticket deferral `budget`, and the backlog path in
283	`ticket_plan.yaml` using the schema in `deferment.md`.
284	
285	**Create the backlog file only if that path does not already exist.** In a
286	repository that has run epics before, the configured backlog path is very often
287	a **cumulative** ledger carrying every prior epic's findings, and writing the
288	empty template over it is a silent, pushable data loss that no validator, test
289	or gate in this workflow detects:
290	
291	```bash
292	test -e <backlog-path> || printf 'findings: []\n' > <backlog-path>
293	```
294	
295	**When the file already exists, do not truncate, re-template, prune, reorder or
296	"reset it for this epic".** Leave every existing row in place and append this
297	epic's findings to it — the `filed_as` references in sealed close-history
298	records point into that file by ID, and rewriting it breaks them. Confirm before
299	dispatching any issue that the row count did not fall:
300	
301	```bash
302	grep -c '^  - id:' <backlog-path>   # before the kickoff commit, and after it
303	```
304	
305	If the epic genuinely needs a backlog scoped to itself, give it a **new path**
306	and record that path in `ticket_plan.yaml`; do not repoint an existing
307	cumulative ledger at a fresh file.
308	
309	Read `references/deferment.md` for scope classification, entry format, agent
310	behavior, and triage.
311	
312	## 4b. Agree the review cadence
313	
314	The third required decision, asked in the same conversation as the goals and the
315	deferment policy. It settles who merges ticket PRs into the epic branch and when
316	the user is handed a review — which is also when they get their only look at the
317	epic while it can still be steered cheaply.
318	
319	Ask once, concretely:
320	
321	> Between waves I'll merge the wave's ticket PRs into the epic branch, then stop
322	> and hand you a review — hot spots in what landed, the decisions I made without
323	> asking and any guardrail that got overridden, where I think the bugs are, what
324	> the epic's own machinery should become, and what I recommend next — with a
325	> rendered diff and a short walkthrough. Should I stop for you at every wave
326	> boundary (recommended), only after named waves, or only at finalization? And
327	> do you want to do the merges yourself instead?
328	
329	Record the answer next to `deferment_policy`:
330	
331	```yaml
332	review_policy:
333	  cadence: wave                 # wave | ticket | milestone | finalization-only
334	  gate: true                    # false: produce the artifact and keep dispatching
335	  merges: owner                 # owner | human
336	  milestones: []                # waves to review after, when cadence is milestone
337	  artifact_root: "results/epic-<slug>/review"
338	  walkthrough: required         # required | on-request
339	```
340	
341	`cadence: finalization-only` and `gate: false` are legitimate for a small or
342	exploratory epic, and both are decisions on the record rather than silence — the
343	epic PR states which policy was in force. The validator warns when the block is
344	missing and errors on a malformed one.
345	
346	Read `references/human-review.md` for what the artifact carries, how the diff is
347	rendered, and what a review may and may not change.
348	
349	## 5. Validate the schedule
350	
351	Treat `depends_on` as a directed graph and reject the plan unless:
352	
353	- every referenced ticket exists and no ticket depends on itself;
354	- a topological ordering includes every ticket;
355	- `blocks` is the reverse of `depends_on`;
356	- tickets in the same wave have no dependency path between them;
357	- every dependency is in an earlier wave;
358	- tickets in the same wave have disjoint conflict keys;
359	- every ticket has an exact validation matrix or an explicit `N/A` reason;
360	- `promotion_order` is unique and total;
361	- promotion order is a topological extension of `depends_on`;
362	- each `promotion_predecessor` names the preceding ticket in that total order;
363	- every ticket relates to at least one declared goal, every goal has a
364	  contributing ticket, and each goal's evaluation ticket both depends on and
365	  promotes after every contributor.
366	
367	Run the bundled validator before dispatch and whenever the schedule changes:
368	
369	```bash
370	uv run <git-epic-workflow-skill>/scripts/validate_epic_plan.py \
371	  specs/desired_program_model/ticket_plan.yaml
372	```
373	
374	Only a plan that cannot be scheduled at all fails (exit 1): no tickets, an
375	unusable or duplicate ticket ID, a `depends_on` naming a ticket that does not
376	exist, or a dependency cycle. Every other rule above is advisory: it prints a
377	`WARNING:` summary (at most three lines; `--verbose` lists all) and exits 0.
378	Read the warnings and fix what matters; do not let them stop the epic. `--strict`
379	turns every rule back into an error. `--force` (or `SKILL_GATES=off`) exits 0
380	even past a blocking error, for when you have decided it does not apply.
381	
382	A valid plan is not a valid dispatch. The plan is this skill's; the assignment
383	block that reaches a ticket agent is rendered by `git-issue` into a GitHub issue
384	body, and a field this plan carries can simply fail to arrive. Validate what
385	GitHub actually holds, per issue, before handing out its URL:
386	
387	```bash
388	gh issue view <issue-number> --json body -q .body \
389	  | uv run <git-epic-workflow-skill>/scripts/validate_assignment.py \
390	      --expect-ticket <stable-ticket-id> --expect-epic-branch epic/<slug>
391	```
392	
393	Exit 2 means there is no parseable assignment block at all; exit 1 lists what is
394	wrong with the one there is. It catches the failures that are invisible in
395	review of the plan: a placeholder nobody rendered, a `pr_base` that is not the
396	epic branch, a `review.mode` other than `external`, a `deferment` block the
397	renderer never learned to emit. Re-run it after any resume that rewrites
398	assignments, because a resume edits issues rather than the plan.
399	
400	The total promotion order is an integration lane, not an implementation
401	dependency. Agents in one wave may implement and validate concurrently, but
402	only the next ticket in that lane may reconcile, close/promote, and enter the
403	epic branch.
404	
405	## 5a. Retire dispatched scope without claiming delivery
406	
407	Retirement is a reviewed schedule amendment for work the owner has explicitly
408	removed from this epic. It is not ticket completion and it does not rewrite the
409	published plan. Use it only after the user chooses the disposition; do not
410	infer abandonment from an idle branch or absent PR.
411	
412	Apply one retirement transaction as follows:
413	
414	1. Reconcile a clean epic worktree at the canonical plan tip. Determine the
415	   complete affected set: the unwanted ticket, every still-active dependent,
416	   its active promotion successor, its evaluation ticket, and every goal it
417	   contributes to or owns. An undelivered non-retired ticket may not depend on,
418	   block, or name a retired ticket as `promotion_predecessor`.
419	2. Preserve every dispatched ticket entry at its original zero-based list
420	   ordinal. Never delete, reorder, rename, or reuse its ID. Increment the root
421	   `schedule_revision` once for the amendment and update every changed active
422	   assignment to that revision.
423	3. Add `status: retired` and the `retirement` block below. Retain the retired
424	   entry's original scheduling fields as history. Do not rewrite a delivered
425	   ticket's sealed historical dependency, reverse-block, or promotion edges,
426	   even when they name a ticket this later amendment retires. Rebuild only the
427	   still-undelivered dependency/reverse-block and promotion-predecessor chains
428	   so new work skips all retired entries; retire or fully deliver every
429	   remaining ticket associated with an affected goal.
430	4. Update GitHub blocking relationships and the marker-delimited assignments
431	   for non-retired tickets to mirror the amended plan. Close or annotate a
432	   retired issue as not planned and link its successor when carried. Never
433	   describe it as merged or implemented.
434	5. Validate the amended plan, then generate each receipt with
435	   `tla-spec-dev --spec-root specs retire ticket <ticket-id>`. Do not hand-write
436	   the receipt manifest. Validate again and review the amendment before commit.
437	
438	The plan entry has this exact shape:
439	
440	```yaml
441	- id: EPIC-4                    # original ID at original ordinal; never moved
442	  status: retired
443	  # ...original scheduling and goal-relation fields remain...
444	  retirement:
445	    schedule_revision: 2       # positive decision revision; <= current root
446	    resolution: carried        # carried | superseded | abandoned
447	    reason: "Owner moved remote hardening out of the local MVP."
448	    decided_by: "@epic-owner"
449	    decided_at: "2026-08-12T03:00:00Z"
450	    successor_issue: "https://github.com/org/repo/issues/99"   # carried only
451	    successor_workflow: "agent-trace-indexing"                 # carried only
452	    receipt: "specs/.history/<workflow>/retired-ticket-003-EPIC-4/manifest.json"
453	    affected_goals:
454	      - goal: GOAL-remote-hardening
455	        disposition: carried   # accepted_missed | accepted_unmeasured | carried
456	        reason: "The local MVP intentionally does not decide this goal."
457	        successor_issue: "https://github.com/org/repo/issues/99" # carried only
458	        successor_workflow: "agent-trace-indexing"               # carried only
459	```
460	
461	`resolution` records what happened to the ticket scope: `carried` moves it to a
462	named issue and workflow, `superseded` says another decision made this ticket's
463	slice unnecessary, and `abandoned` says the owner deliberately drops it. A
464	carried ticket requires both top-level successor fields, every affected goal
465	must also be `carried`, and every goal must name that exact same successor issue
466	and workflow. A superseded or abandoned ticket has no successor fields, none of
467	its affected goals may be carried, and non-carried goal entries have no
468	successor fields. Ticket and goals move together or do not carry at all. None
469	of the resolution values is a direct ticket `status`; the only schedule state
470	for this transaction is `retired`.
471	
472	`retirement.schedule_revision` seals the revision at which the owner made this
473	decision. It equals the root revision when the receipt is created, but a later
474	unrelated plan amendment may advance the root beyond it. Never rewrite the
475	retirement block merely to catch up: validation requires a positive decision
476	revision no newer than the current root, and the receipt must continue to match
477	the complete decision-time `retirement` mapping exactly.
478	
479	`affected_goals` must exactly copy every goal the ticket relates to or owns,
480	including a goal for which it was the evaluator. `accepted_missed` records that
481	the owner accepts a known miss; `accepted_unmeasured` records that the owner
482	accepts closing without a measurement; `carried` requires its own named
483	successor issue and workflow. When several retired tickets affect one goal,
484	their dispositions and carried target must agree, in addition to matching each
485	ticket-level decision. Do not delete the goal or edit its baseline/target to
486	conceal the disposition.
487	
488	The canonical receipt path encodes the immutable zero-based ordinal and ID:
489	
490	```text
491	specs/.history/<workflow>/retired-ticket-<ordinal:03d>-<safe-id>/manifest.json
492	```
493	
494	For a git-epic workflow, `specs/.history` is canonical and the plan receipt must
495	use that exact repository-relative prefix. The lower-level `tla-spec-dev` CLI
496	may support a custom history root for non-epic workflows; that flexibility does
497	not change the epic contract.
498	
499	The generated manifest identifies both `kind` and `entry_kind` as
500	`ticket-retirement`, and asserts `semantic_promotion.performed: false` and
501	`validation.claimed: false`. It is a durable receipt that work was *not*
502	accepted or measured, not a close-history entry. A delivered PR/history cannot
503	substitute for this receipt, and this receipt cannot substitute for delivery
504	evidence. If an abandoned ticket workspace existed, the retire command may
505	archive it as explicitly unaccepted; that archive is not a promoted model.
506	The plan and receipt declaration are closed schemas: do not add extension keys
507	to `retirement` or its `affected_goals` entries, and do not reorder or edit the
508	declaration after the receipt exists.
509	
510	Prefer an amendment/reconciliation ticket over assigning shared workflow-wide
511	metadata to a parallel ticket. Ticket agents own their plan entry and declared
512	semantic slice; the epic owner owns ticket order, dependency edges, and
513	workflow-wide status.
514	
515	## 6. Create or schedule GitHub issues
516	
517	Every scheduled issue maps to one spec ticket and retains the standard
518	`git-issue` sections: Summary, References, Discovery notes, Worktree & branch,
519	Spec workflow, and Regression & close-out.
520	
521	### New issues
522	
523	Use `git-issue` to create the work order, then add the assignment from
524	`epic-ticket.md`. Set the spec workflow to REQUIRED because the agent must open
525	and close its planned spec ticket. If a slice has no semantic delta, document
526	the no-op model result and its evidence; do not silently skip ticket closeout.
527	
528	After issue creation, write its URL back to `ticket_plan.yaml` and update the
529	assignment with the final issue number, feature branch, and worktree path.
530	Commit and push the canonical plan, then record that commit plus the current
531	`schedule_revision` in every assignment.
532	
533	### Existing issues
534	
535	Read the existing body and preserve it. Add or replace only this bounded region:
536	
537	```text
538	<!-- git-epic-workflow:assignment:start -->
539	...rendered assignment from epic-ticket.md...
540	<!-- git-epic-workflow:assignment:end -->
541	```
542	
543	Use `gh issue edit --body-file`; do not append duplicate assignments on resume.
544	The assignment explicitly overrides any older instruction to branch from or
545	target the default branch.
546	
547	### Mirror the dependency DAG in GitHub
548	
549	After every issue number exists, mirror each `depends_on` edge with GitHub's
550	blocking relationship and verify both directions:
551	
552	```bash
553	gh issue edit <ticket-issue> --add-blocked-by <dependency-issue>
554	gh issue view <ticket-issue> --json blockedBy,blocking
555	```
556	
557	On resume, compare the GitHub relationships with `ticket_plan.yaml`; add missing
558	edges and remove stale edges with the corresponding `--remove-blocked-by` /
559	`--remove-blocking` flags. The plan remains canonical, but the tracker must show
560	the same readiness graph agents see in their assignments.
561	
562	Before dispatch, render every assignment from its canonical plan entry and
563	compare the following fields exactly: ticket ID, schedule revision,
564	dependencies, blocks, wave, promotion order/predecessor, conflict keys, goal
565	relations, validation matrix, and evidence root. An older ancestor `plan_commit` alone is
566	not freshness proof; the copied scheduling fields must still match.
567	
568	## 7. Commit, push, and dispatch
569	
570	Review the desired model and plan, then commit and push `epic/<slug>` before
571	dispatch. Each assignment records an epic base SHA that is already reachable
572	from the remote epic branch.
573	
574	Return the goals the epic is aiming at:
575	
576	| Goal | Kind | Metric | Baseline | Target | Decided by |
577	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
578	
579	and a schedule such as:
580	
581	| Issue | Spec ticket | Start dependencies | Wave | Promote after | Goals | State |
582	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
583	
584	An issue is ready to hand off only when every dependency PR is merged into the
585	remote epic branch. An open or green PR is not a satisfied dependency.
586	
587	Whenever you recommend the next ticket — at dispatch and on every resume — read
588	the deferred-findings backlog and present pending entries in the same report.
589	From the first wave boundary onward that report is a section of the wave review
590	artifact rather than a separate message (`references/human-review.md` §3.5); the
591	table and the three outcomes are the same either way:
592	
593	| ID | Found by | Severity | Summary | Blast radius | Disposition |
594	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
595	
596	Ask the user, per pending finding, to promote it to a ticket now, keep it
597	batched, or close it `wontfix`. Recommend batching unless it blocks a planned
598	ticket. Promoting a finding is a plan change: new stable ID, dependency edges,
599	wave, promotion order, conflict keys, revalidated schedule, bumped
600	`schedule_revision`, new issue. Never retrofit it into a dispatched ticket.
601	
602	This version does not start agents or poll them. The user passes ready issue
603	URLs to ticket agents, then invokes the epic workflow again to integrate and
604	review the finished wave, refresh readiness, or finalize. Merging those tickets'
605	PRs into the epic branch is this skill's work, not the user's, unless
606	`review_policy.merges` says `human` (`references/human-review.md` §1).
